how-much-to-charge-for-a-flat-roof.html.text:
Flat roof bid calculator

How much to charge for a flat roof

A published “$650 a square” special prices the plan. A TPO or EPDM roof is not that number. It is a membrane mil that does not scale with squares, a recover or a tear-off, dry insulation or wet, and lineal feet of parapet the coupon never counted. Matching the coupon on an 80-mil TPO tear-off is how a sold job becomes unpaid welding time after the first parapet.

Open the free bid calculator

The number a per-square special cannot see

Take a 40×30 garage, TPO 45-mil, recover, two drains, no parapet. That is 1,200 plan square feet and 12 squares — 12.96 membrane squares after 8% waste. The coupon says about $7,800. Raise the same shop to an 80×50 two-story commercial deck at 1/2" per foot. The plan is 4,000 square feet, so the coupon says about $26,026 on 40.04 squares. The job did not scale that way: 80-mil membrane, a welder, a wet-insulation tear-off, two polyiso layers, 80 lineal feet of parapet, six drains, and four HVAC curbs the garage never had.

Put EPDM on that garage. Sheets now cost more per square the TPO-45 recover never priced. Two stories are not “the same squares plus a ladder.” A parapet is not in the square number at all.

How to price it

  1. Measure building length and width.
  2. Apply the slope: 1/4" per foot is 1.000, 1" per foot is 1.003. Roof squares are that area ÷ 100.
  3. Count membrane squares after kit waste and extra waste from parapet flashing. Recover tear-off is zero. A full tear-off covers the roof.
  4. Price membrane (TPO 45 / 60 / 80, EPDM, modified bitumen, PVC), insulation layers, parapet, drains, curbs, walk pads, cover board, and the permit allowance.
  5. Load the wage, add materials and mobilization, mark overhead on direct cost, then divide by one minus the target margin. The walk-away price is total cost.

The flat roof bid calculator does that arithmetic in the browser from your own hours and invoices. Starting waste, hours, and material rates are ballpark figures to replace, not a catalog or a code table.

What this is not

This is not a building-code opinion, a permit, a construction specification, a wind-uplift rating, or an engineering stamp. Confirm the jurisdiction and a qualified professional before sending a price. The output is arithmetic on the numbers you typed.

No warranty. This free article and calculator are not construction, legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from their use. Hosted URLs, when they exist, may be taken offline without notice; there is no availability SLA.

Common questions

How much to charge for a flat roof?

Start from the building plan, apply the low-slope factor to get roof squares, then count membrane squares after waste, tear-off, insulation layers, parapet flashing, drains, and the permit. A published $650 per square special only sees plan squares.

Why do TPO 80-mil and a tear-off change the price?

A 40-by-30 garage is 12 squares of TPO-45 recover. An 80-by-50 two-story commercial deck is 40.04 squares of 80-mil TPO, a wet-insulation tear-off, two polyiso layers, 80 lineal feet of parapet, and six drains. Matching the garage coupon is how the commercial job loses money.

Is this a building-code calculation?

No. Membrane rates, waste, and insulation figures here are common starting points on residential and light-commercial bids. They are not a building-code opinion, a permit, a wind-uplift rating, or an engineering stamp.

    Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

    Common questions

    Why can a competitor advertise “$650 a square”?

    Usually because the special is written around one specific job, and that job is a preset here: a 12-square TPO-45 recover over an existing membrane on a one-story garage. It really does price low. What the per-square number cannot see is recover versus tear-off, wet insulation, parapet flashing, drains, curbs, and story count. Price your actual roof beside the special and the gap becomes a list of line items instead of an argument about who is honest.

    Why does a tear-off cost so much more than a recover for the same square footage?

    A recover installs new membrane over what is already up there. A tear-off strips the old roof down to deck first — labor and disposal that a recover skips entirely. Adding wet insulation on top of that means replacing waterlogged polyiso discovered under the old membrane, which is exactly the kind of cost a flat per-square special from a garage recover was never priced to cover.

    Why do parapet walls, drains, and curbs get their own line items?

    Because they are flashed and sealed individually, not spread across the field membrane. Eighty linear feet of parapet on a commercial building is eighty feet of detail work at the wall-to-roof transition. Each roof drain and HVAC curb is its own penetration that has to be flashed watertight. None of that scales with plan squares the way flat field membrane does.

    Does this check building code, wind-uplift rating, or engineering requirements?

    No. Membrane rates, waste, and insulation figures here are common starting points for residential and light-commercial bids, not a building-code opinion, a permit, a wind-uplift rating, or an engineering stamp. Confirm the jurisdiction and a qualified professional before sending a price, especially on multi-story or high-wind-zone work.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your bid is saved in this browser’s local storage so it is still here next visit, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your roof dimensions, wages, or prices.

    What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

    The bid price already includes your target margin on top of labor, materials, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — membrane, tear-off, insulation, parapet, drains, curbs, and permit — the point below which the job stops being profitable at all. Typing a price you are considering shows you the margin or the loss before you send it.

vs-a-flat-650-per-square-special.html.text:
← Flat Roof Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $650 per square special

"$650 a square" is not a price for a flat roof — it is a price for one specific roof, usually a small recover, quietly applied to every roof that calls for a quote.

What a flat per-square special is

A flat per-square number is the fastest thing a company can put on an ad or a postcard: one rate, times the plan squares, read back as a total. It is also the unit homeowners and property managers already compare between competing bids.

The rate was set for one job — commonly a small, one-story recover over an existing membrane, with no tear-off, no wet insulation, little or no parapet, and few penetrations — and then quoted to the next caller, whether or not that roof shares any of those.

What this calculator does instead

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the membrane, scope, slope, stories, plan length and width, parapet, drains, HVAC curbs, walk pads, and polyiso layers, plus your own wage, payroll burden, membrane and insulation cost, dumpster, mobilization, permit, overhead, and target margin. It turns that into membrane squares after waste, tear-off and insulation squares, crew hours by task, and a price — for this roof, not a rate carried over from the last one.

What a flat per-square special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate for a membrane recover and a full tear-off of the identical plan squares, even though tear-off is its own labor and dumpster line the recover never had. Prices recover, tear-off, and tear-off-plus-insulation as their own scope, with tear-off hours, dumpster cost, and insulation hours and material priced separately.
Has no line for parapet flashing — a flat roof with no walls and one with 80 lf of parapet detail get the same rate. Prices parapet hours and material by the lineal foot, and adds extra membrane waste for parapet flashing on top of the base kit waste.
Has no line for roof drains, HVAC curbs, or walk pads — each is its own flashed penetration or protected walkway, not a fraction of a blended rate. Prices drains, curbs, and walk pads as their own hour and material lines, by count or by square.
Has no line for stories or access — a one-story garage and a two-story commercial deck of the same plan squares get the same rate. Adds extra hours per square for a second or third story, so height and access show up in the price instead of being absorbed into it.
Gives the crew a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price per square and the walk-away price alongside the total, so a shopped rate can be scored against real cost before you match it.

The special's own job, and a job it was never priced for

Using this calculator's own two built-in presets and its own shipped shop-rate defaults — $36 hourly wage, 32% burden, 15% overhead, 25% target margin:

The 12-square TPO-45 recover on a one-story garage (a 40×30 ft plan, two drains, no parapet, no tear-off, no insulation — the job a $650-a-square special is usually built around) takes 23.5 crew-hours and this calculator prices it at $6,527.72 for the job — $543.98 per square, under the $650 headline rate once labor, membrane, and a target margin are actually counted.

The 40.04-square TPO-80 tear-off (an 80×50 ft commercial plan, two layers of polyiso insulation, 80 lf of parapet, six drains, and four HVAC curbs) is a different job at roughly three times the plan squares. It takes 245.3 crew-hours — more than ten times the recover's labor — costs $47,934.71 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $63,912.94. Quoting that job at the flat $650-a-square rate reproduces $26,026.00 for the job, which is $21,908.71 below its own break-even cost — before counting the $37,886.94 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 25% target margin. Same unit, same headline rate, one roof that pays and one that loses money before the first parapet seam is welded.

Common questions

Why does a flat $650 per square special get a flat-roof bid wrong?

Because a roofing square (100 sq ft) only measures plan area, not what the job takes to close in. A 12-square TPO-45 recover on a one-story garage -- no tear-off, no insulation, two drains, no parapet -- takes about 23.5 crew-hours on this calculator's own preset. A 40-square commercial tear-off with two layers of polyiso, 80 lf of parapet, six drains, and four HVAC curbs takes about 245.3 crew-hours -- more than ten times the labor at roughly three times the plan squares -- because recover-versus-tear-off, insulation, and parapet detail never show up in a per-square number.

What job is the $650-a-square number actually built around?

One specific job, usually the easiest one a company is willing to advertise: a small, one-story recover over an existing membrane, with no tear-off, no wet insulation, little or no parapet, and few penetrations. It is a marketing price meant to get the phone to ring, not a number derived from any particular building's scope, insulation, or detail work.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs on its own two built-in presets: the 12-square TPO-45 recover prices at $6,527.72 for the job -- $543.98 per square, under the $650 headline rate. The 40.04-square TPO-80 tear-off with two layers of polyiso, 80 lf of parapet, six drains, and four HVAC curbs costs $47,934.71 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $63,912.94. Quoting that job at the flat $650-a-square rate reproduces $26,026.00 for the job -- $21,908.71 below its own break-even cost, before counting the $37,886.94 it falls short of this calculator's price at a 25% target margin.

Is a flat per-square special ever a reasonable shorthand?

For a narrow band of jobs close to the one the special was priced on -- a similar recover, similar membrane, little or no parapet, few penetrations -- a per-square number can land close. The risk is quoting a tear-off, added insulation, or a run of parapet flashing the same way sight unseen, because the rate does not know the scope until the roof is actually measured, and by then the per-square number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or material costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market or your supplier's membrane, insulation, or flashing pricing. It takes the membrane, scope, slope, stories, plan dimensions, parapet, drains, curbs, and insulation you enter, and your own wage, payroll burden, membrane and insulation cost, dumpster, mobilization, permit, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into crew hours and a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat per-square special skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat per-square special is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest way to advertise that works until the roof stops matching the one the special was priced on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it. The $6,527.72, $543.98, $47,934.71, and $63,912.94 figures above are this calculator's own arithmetic on its own built-in preset list (open the calculator and pick a starting job from the list to reproduce them), not a claim about any specific contractor's real costs or any specific company's advertised price.

vs-acculynx.html.text:
← Flat Roof Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. AccuLynx

Two different shapes: AccuLynx is an account-based platform for running a roofing company's whole sales-to-production pipeline. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one low-slope roof cost, given its membrane, its scope, its insulation, and its parapet, before you send the bid.

What each tool is for

AccuLynx is a cloud-based business management platform built specifically for roofing contractors, headquartered in Beloit, Wisconsin. It is built around running a roofing company's whole pipeline in one account: lead capture and CRM, aerial roof measurement, estimating and proposal generation, material ordering with supplier integrations, production and crew scheduling, and job costing, used by a sales team, a production manager, and office staff together across every job the company runs, on an ongoing subscription. It is a large enough business in that niche that in July 2025 Verisk Analytics — the NYSE-listed insurance-data and analytics company — signed a definitive agreement to acquire it in an all-cash deal valued at $2.35 billion, a deal a Delaware Chancery Court later ordered Verisk to complete after a dispute over its regulatory review. AccuLynx's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity, category, and the acquisition — reported by Verisk's own newsroom and multiple trade and financial press outlets — are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no subscription price for it appears on this page.

This calculator does none of that. It does not track a lead, order material, schedule a crew, or hold a record across jobs. It takes one low-slope roof — the membrane kit (TPO 45/60/80-mil, EPDM 60-mil, PVC 60-mil, or two-ply modified bitumen), the scope (recover over existing membrane, full tear-off to deck, or tear-off plus wet insulation), slope and stories, the building's plan length and width converted to roof squares and membrane squares after kit and parapet waste, polyiso insulation layers, parapet flashing by the lineal foot, roof drains, HVAC curbs, walk-pad squares, cover board, loaded labor, mobilization, dumpster, permit, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep — and turns that into the job price, the price per square, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, plus a printable customer proposal with a deposit split and a price-held date. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a lead record, a material order, or a building-code determination.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Should I use this calculator or AccuLynx?

They do different jobs. AccuLynx, headquartered in Beloit, Wisconsin, is a cloud-based, roofing-only business management platform used by residential and commercial roofing contractors to run a company's whole sales-to-production pipeline: lead and CRM tracking, aerial measurement and estimating, proposal generation, material ordering, production and crew scheduling, and job costing, tied to one account used on an ongoing subscription basis across every job the company runs. It takes one flat-roof job's membrane (TPO 45/60/80-mil, EPDM, PVC, or modified bitumen), scope (recover, tear-off, or tear-off plus wet insulation), slope, stories, plan length and width, membrane and parapet waste, polyiso layers, parapet flashing, roof drains, HVAC curbs, walk pads, cover board, loaded labor, mobilization, dump, permit, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the job price, the price per square, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, plus a printable customer proposal, instantly, with no account and nothing uploaded.
